after: ## Why reflection is a separate skill
alt: AO2 Reflection is weighted at 22% of Component 2, the Essay, against 0% in the Written Exam. Below, the five Critical Path questions: viewpoint before research, how it relates to the perspectives, the impact of the research, why it had that effect, and what further research might help.
caption: Reflection is a fifth of the Essay mark, so it needs more than a closing sentence.

alt: Five steps: state your starting point, name the perspective that challenged or confirmed it, say whether your view was strengthened, qualified or reversed, give the specific argument or evidence that caused this, and suggest what would test your new view. Step 4, the reason, is highlighted as earning most credit.
caption: The reason your view moved, step 4, is where most of the credit lies.

after: ## Three ways a view can move
alt: A starting view meets the strongest opposing case and ends up strengthened, qualified or reversed. Strengthened means explaining why the opposing argument did not persuade; qualified means the view holds only in some conditions; reversed means naming the argument or evidence that changed it.
caption: Any of the three outcomes counts as reflection, provided you give the reason.

after: ## Where reflection goes in the essay
alt: An essay strip from introduction to conclusion with reflective moments marked: one in the introduction stating the starting view, several within the evaluation as each perspective is weighed, and one in the conclusion giving the personal supported view, the reason it moved or held, and the limits of the research.
caption: Reflection is woven through the essay, not saved for the final sentence.

after: ## Reflecting on the limits of your research
alt: Four kinds of limit, coverage, type of evidence, your own standpoint and unresolved disagreement between credible sources, each lead to a consequence statement: so my conclusion applies more confidently to one case than to another.
caption: Name a limit, then say what it does to your conclusion.

alt: A strong suggestion has three parts, each with an example: what (household surveys from rural areas of countries that have introduced the policy), why (my sources are mostly from cities), and how it could change the judgement (the conclusion might need to be limited to cities). “More research is needed” fails all three.
caption: Say what to research, why, and how the result could change your judgement.

alt: For the question on compulsory voting, the weak reflection only says the writer can see both sides. The strong reflection covers every step: a starting view, the liberty-based argument that challenged it, a qualified view, the reason (turnout evidence, but only with a none-of-the-above option), a limit in the countries studied, and specific comparative research.
caption: The strong version names what moved the writer and how far.
